claims.text: Baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
Baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
Baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 has approximately 13.5% terminal tensile strain at room temperature under quasi-static loading.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has established energetic performance under impact conditions.
Adding approximately 1–2 at.% Nb to HfZrTiTa0.53 will promote nanoscale ductile precipitates.
Adding approximately 1–2 at.% Nb to HfZrTiTa0.53 will cause beneficial Nb segregation at grain boundaries and improve grain-boundary structure.
Nb microalloying will encourage nucleation of ductile secondary phases at grain boundaries.
The proposed precipitates or grain-boundary modification will delay localized necking during tensile deformation.
The proposed precipitates or grain-boundary modification will delay crack initiation during tensile deformation.
Nb addition will improve tensile ductility and uniform elongation by 30–50%, reaching roughly 18–20%.
The Nb-modified alloy's yield strength will remain within ±5% of 786 MPa.
The Nb-modified alloy's compressive strength will remain within ±5% of 1314 MPa.
The Nb addition will cause no reduction in impact-triggered energy release.
The predicted benefits apply in uniaxial tension and compression at approximately 10^-3 s^-1 from room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures.
The predicted preservation of energetic performance applies to impacts comparable to thin-steel-target penetration.
The dispersion, stability, and efficacy of the proposed Nb-induced microstructure depend on alloying homogeneity and thermomechanical processing.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% baseline is identified as terminal tensile strain, but the predicted outcome treats it as the baseline uniform elongation. Terminal strain and uniform elongation are distinct tensile metrics, so the claimed 30–50% comparison is not internally metric-matched.
